topic: Sound for Picture — Post Workflow & Deliverables

fields.definition: The process of reducing or removing unwanted room reverberation and reflections from recorded dialogue, typically using spectral or algorithmic dereverb processing, to improve clarity and intelligibility.
fields.plain_english: This means taking the echoey room sound out of recorded speech. It makes a voice sound clear and close, as if it were captured in a quiet booth instead of a big empty room.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to rescue location dialogue recorded in echoey spaces so it cuts through the mix and matches quieter studio or ADR lines.
fields.practical_application: A dialogue editor runs a dereverb plug-in such as iZotope RX De-reverb on a scene shot in a hard-walled room, dialing in reduction until the voice is clear without sounding hollow.
common_mistakes: Over-processing until the voice sounds hollow, robotic, or underwater
Expecting dereverb to fully replace a bad recording rather than reduce reverb
Applying one static setting across a scene instead of adjusting per line
Confusing dereverberation with noise reduction, which targets a different problem
scenario_contexts: Cleaning up dialogue shot in an empty tiled bathroom or stairwell
Matching a reverberant wide-shot take to a tighter close-up take
Preparing echoey location dialogue to sit alongside dry ADR lines

sources: iZotope RX technical documentation
Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers

fields.definition: A mix control that spreads center-panned dialogue partly into the left and right channels, so a signal placed in the center is also reproduced by the adjacent speakers rather than solely by the center channel.
fields.plain_english: Normally movie dialogue comes only from the middle speaker. Divergence lets some of that voice also play from the left and right speakers, so it feels wider and does not vanish if you sit off to one side.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to keep center dialogue audible and stable across a wide seating area and to blend the voice into the front sound field instead of pinning it to one speaker.
fields.practical_application: A re-recording mixer adds a small amount of divergence to spread dialogue across the front three channels, or uses it so a phantom center still works when the center speaker is weak.
common_mistakes: Adding too much divergence, which smears the dialogue image and weakens its anchor to the screen
Assuming divergence and ordinary panning do the same thing
Forgetting how divergence interacts with downmix and phantom-center behavior
scenario_contexts: Spreading dialogue across left, center, and right for a wide theatrical seating area
Keeping dialogue feeling centered when a center speaker is small or absent
Blending narration into the front field in a surround mix

sources: Dolby technical documentation
Holman, Sound for Film and Television

fields.definition: The deliberate addition of discrete delay repeats to a dialogue line as a creative effect, used to signal a memory, dream, hallucination, large space, or supernatural quality rather than to correct a recording.
fields.plain_english: This is adding repeats to a character's voice on purpose, so the words bounce back like a shout in a canyon. It is used for dreams, memories, or spooky moments, not to fix a bad recording.
fields.purpose_function: It exists as a storytelling tool to mark that a voice is inside a character's head, in a huge space, or otherworldly.
fields.practical_application: A mixer sends a flashback line to a delay plug-in and blends in timed repeats, often filtered, so the words echo without becoming impossible to understand.
common_mistakes: Setting the echo so loud or long that the words become impossible to understand
Using a raw delay with no filtering, so the effect sounds cheap
Overusing the effect until it loses its dramatic impact
scenario_contexts: A dream or flashback sequence
A god-like or ghostly voice
A memory replaying a past line of dialogue

sources: Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound
Holman, Sound for Film and Television

fields.definition: The application of equalization to dialogue tracks to shape their tonal balance, reducing problem frequencies such as low-end rumble, proximity boom, sibilance, or boxiness and adding presence, so lines are clear, consistent, and intelligible.
fields.plain_english: This is adjusting the tone of recorded speech by turning some pitch ranges up and others down. It removes booming or harsh sounds and adds clarity, like tuning the bass and treble so a voice is easy to understand.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to make dialogue intelligible and tonally even from shot to shot, and to help voices cut through music and effects without becoming harsh.
fields.practical_application: A dialogue mixer high-passes rumble, dips a boxy low-mid, and adds a gentle presence lift so a boomy location line matches the rest of the scene.
common_mistakes: Boosting instead of cutting, causing a harsh or unnatural tone
Not high-passing low-frequency rumble and handling noise
Applying one EQ across a whole scene instead of matching shot to shot
Over-brightening until sibilance turns harsh
scenario_contexts: Removing proximity boom from a close boom take
Matching the tone of a lav mic to a boom mic on the same line
Helping dialogue sit clearly over a loud music cue

sources: Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers
iZotope RX technical documentation
Holman, Sound for Film and Television

fields.definition: The use of downward expansion or gating on dialogue to reduce the level of background noise, room tone, and bleed during pauses between words or lines, lowering signal below a threshold while leaving speech largely untouched.
fields.plain_english: This quietly turns down the gaps between spoken words, where only background noise sits. The voice stays full, but hiss and room noise drop when nobody is talking, like muting the mic between lines.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to clean up the spaces around dialogue so noise does not pile up when many tracks play together, without dulling the speech itself.
fields.practical_application: An editor sets an expander threshold just below the quietest words so background hiss drops in the pauses, then checks that word beginnings and endings are not chopped off.
common_mistakes: Setting the threshold too high, which clips off soft word starts and endings
Using heavy expansion instead of proper noise reduction, causing pumping
Forgetting that abrupt gating makes room tone jump on and off unnaturally
scenario_contexts: Reducing air-conditioning hiss between lines of dialogue
Cleaning bleed on a multi-mic dialogue scene
Tightening noisy lav-mic tracks before the final mix

sources: Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers
iZotope RX technical documentation

fields.definition: The intentional processing of dialogue to sound as though it is reproduced through a limited-fidelity device such as a telephone, radio, television, intercom, or PA, typically by band-limiting the frequency response and adding distortion or noise to match the source shown on screen.
fields.plain_english: Futzing means making a voice sound like it comes out of a phone, radio, or TV. You cut the deep and high tones and add a little grit, so it matches the small speaker the audience sees on screen.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to make off-screen or device-sourced voices believable, so a phone or radio voice truly seems to come from that device.
fields.practical_application: A mixer band-passes a line, adds slight distortion and maybe a codec or noise layer, and automates it so the futz starts exactly when a character raises a phone to their ear.
common_mistakes: Making the futz so extreme that the words become impossible to understand
Failing to match the futz to the on-screen device, such as a tiny phone versus a large PA
Not automating the effect so it starts and stops with the picture
Leaving the futzed line as wide and full as normal dialogue
scenario_contexts: A phone call heard from only one character's side
A voice over a two-way radio or intercom
A news anchor heard from a TV in the background

sources: Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound
Holman, Sound for Film and Television

fields.definition: The application of a limiter to dialogue to cap short-term peaks and control dynamic range, preventing overloads and keeping levels consistent so speech stays within target loudness and does not clip or jump out of the mix.
fields.plain_english: A limiter puts a ceiling on how loud the voice can get. It catches sudden loud words so nothing overloads, keeping speech steady and even, like a safety lid that stops peaks from spilling over.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to guard against clipping and to keep dialogue level even, so quiet and loud lines both sit within the loudness targets required for delivery.
fields.practical_application: A mixer places a limiter on the dialogue bus to catch stray peaks after compression, setting the ceiling below full scale so the stem stays clean and meets delivery loudness specs.
common_mistakes: Over-limiting until dialogue sounds squashed and lifeless
Using a limiter to do the job of gain riding or compression
Watching only peaks while ignoring loudness delivery standards
UNSAFE: monitoring at excessive SPL for long sessions to judge peaks, risking noise-induced hearing loss; observe OSHA exposure limits
scenario_contexts: Catching plosive peaks before the dialogue stem
Meeting a broadcast or streaming loudness and true-peak spec
Keeping dialogue from clipping during a loud emotional line

sources: Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers
Holman, Sound for Film and Television
OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95

fields.definition: The placement of dialogue at a specific perceived position within the stereo or surround sound field, using panning, level, and channel routing so a voice appears to come from the direction of its on-screen source.
fields.plain_english: This means making a voice seem to come from the right spot on the screen. If a character stands on the left, the sound is placed so your ears point that way, matching what your eyes see.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to tie voices to their on-screen sources and hold the audience's attention on the picture, though most lead dialogue is localized to the center for stability.
fields.practical_application: A mixer usually keeps lead dialogue in the center channel but may nudge off-screen or background voices toward their positions when it strengthens the scene without distracting the listener.
common_mistakes: Hard-panning main dialogue to screen position, which distracts and breaks on downmix
Assuming stereo panning translates the same in a theater as on headphones
Ignoring that most narrative dialogue belongs in a stable center image
scenario_contexts: Deciding whether an off-screen voice should be panned to its side
Keeping lead dialogue centered while placing background voices
Matching a moving character's voice to their position across the frame

sources: Holman, Sound for Film and Television
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers

fields.definition: The stage of post-production in which all dialogue elements, including production sound, ADR, and loop group, are balanced, processed, and combined into a coherent, intelligible dialogue stem that sits correctly against music and effects.
fields.plain_english: This is the step where all the spoken lines are balanced and cleaned into one smooth track. The goal is to make every word clear and even, so you never struggle to hear the characters over the music and effects.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to make speech consistently clear and intelligible, since dialogue carries the story and must be understood over everything else in the mix.
fields.practical_application: A dialogue mixer edits, EQs, de-noises, compresses, and rides the level of each line, matching ADR to production sound and delivering a dialogue stem for the final re-recording mix.
common_mistakes: Mixing dialogue too low so it gets buried under music and effects
Failing to match ADR tone and level to the original production sound
Skipping cleanup so noise and inconsistency carry into the final mix
Judging levels without checking delivery loudness targets
scenario_contexts: Balancing production dialogue with ADR replacements in a scene
Building the dialogue stem for a film or episode
Keeping dialogue intelligible under a busy action sequence

sources: Holman, Sound for Film and Television
Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers
